topic.title: Why can't you drive from North to South America?
topic.map_answer: the one gap in the highway's line: about 106 km between Yaviza in Panama and Turbo in Colombia, where the Darién rainforest and the Atrato marshes sit across the border

title: Why does the road from Alaska to Argentina stop in Panama?
description:
One road runs from Alaska to Argentina. Why does it stop dead in Panama?
The Darién Gap, found on the map by driving the Pan-American Highway south until the tarmac runs out.
Sources: Wikipedia, Darién Gap (Nov 2026). The characters are not advisers.
Maps simplified. Borders as recognised by the country each video is about.

lines.text: Why does the road from Alaska to Argentina stop in Panama?
It's the Pan-American Highway: about 30,000 kilometres of road, one line drawn down two whole continents.
Start in Alaska and drive south: through Canada, the United States, Mexico, and down the thin neck of Central America.
Then at Yaviza, a small town in the jungle of eastern Panama, the tarmac simply ends.
The road only starts again at Turbo, in Colombia, about 106 kilometres away. That gap has a name: the Darién Gap.
So what fills it? Steep mountains, thick rainforest, and on the Colombian side, a marsh 80 kilometres wide.
Drivers can't cross it. Instead they put their cars on a ship on Panama's Caribbean coast and sail around the gap to Colombia.
Road builders have drawn plans to close it for decades. So why is the gap still open?
Because the gap is kept on purpose. In 1980, Panama made the jungle a national park: 5,790 square kilometres of protected forest.
And the jungle works as a wall against a cattle disease, foot-and-mouth, keeping it from walking north out of South America to the herds beyond.
Finish the road or keep the jungle: which would you pick? That's why the road from Alaska to Argentina stops in Panama.
